items.title: Georgian England had 200+ capital offences

options.text: A modernised criminal code that abolished hanging
The expansion of capital crimes from around 50 in 1688 to over 220 by 1815 — including stealing goods worth 12 pence from a shop
A medieval system of trial by ordeal
The system of cattle thieves' execution in Scotland only

items.reveal:
The Waltham Black Act (1723) alone created around 50 new capital offences. Many capital sentences were commuted (juries undervalued goods to avoid death penalty — 'pious perjury'), or replaced by transportation to America (until 1776) and Australia (from 1787).

Reformers — Samuel Romilly, Robert Peel as Home Secretary — gradually reduced the list. By 1841 only treason, murder and a handful of others remained capital. Public hangings at Tyburn ended in 1783 (moved to Newgate); the last public hanging was 1868.
items.why: The Bloody Code shows the early modern state using execution as a substitute for an effective police force. The Victorian shift to imprisonment + policing changes the whole structure of criminal justice.

items.title: Anglo-Saxon law replaced revenge with a price list

options.text: A trial by combat for serious crimes
A 'man-price' — compensation paid to a victim's family or to a victim of injury, set by social rank (a king's wergild far higher than a ceorl's) to end blood feuds
A property tax owed to the lord

items.reveal:
Aethelberht's law code (Kent, c. 600 CE) — the earliest surviving English legal text — sets compensation for injuries with itemised precision: four shillings for an outer ear, twelve for the inner. Murder of a freeman (ceorl) was 200 shillings; a thegn 600; a king's son much higher.

Wergild aimed to substitute payment for cyclical feud. It coexisted with the death penalty for some offences (theft, treason). The Norman Conquest gradually replaced wergild with crown justice — crimes against the king's peace rather than against persons.
items.why: 'Justice' has had many shapes. Anglo-Saxon law was rational, written and surprisingly modern in seeing crime as economic harm — but built around social hierarchy in a way modern law explicitly rejects.

items.title: London had no professional police force until 1829
items.claim: Who founded the Metropolitan Police and on what principles?

options.text: Home Secretary Robert Peel, Metropolitan Police Act 1829, with the principle that police derive authority from public consent — Peel's 'nine principles'
The Duke of Wellington as PM, modelled on military regiments

items.reveal:
The Met began with around 1,000 officers based at Scotland Yard. Uniforms were deliberately civilian-looking (blue, not the military red) to distinguish them from soldiers. Officers carried truncheons, not firearms.

The Fielding brothers' Bow Street Runners (1750) had been a small detective force. Peel's innovation was preventive uniformed patrol, full-time and salaried. Within decades every English borough had a force; the County Police Acts of 1839 and 1856 extended it nationwide.

Peel's nine principles — including 'the police are the public and the public are the police' — are still cited.
items.why: Modern policing is younger than the Industrial Revolution. The concept of a professional, preventive, public force is an early 19th-century invention with specific design choices that still shape British policing.
